extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, literary critics, and researchers of humor/wit
extracted.subtask_description: Theoretical criteria for analyzing and producing wit (jokes) from a psychoanalytic/aesthetic perspective, emphasizing technique, tendency, and the pleasure-mechanism behind wit. Useful for literary analysis, humor theory, or crafting jokes with psychological effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and tendency as dual pleasure-sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure created by wit is dependent upon the technique on one hand and upon the tendency on the other hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing a joke, assess both (a) the technical means used (wordplay, absurdity, displacement, allusion, etc.) and (b) the tendency/content (what wish, hostility, cynicism or insight it gratifies). Strong wit typically uses both effectively; weak wit may have technique but no meaningful tendency or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of psychic expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasurable effect of tendency-wit (and many technical devices) corresponds to an 'economy in the expenditure of inhibitions or suppressions'—wit relieves psychic expenditure by removing or avoiding inhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer jokes that enable gratification otherwise stifled by internal or external restraints. Evaluate how the joke reduces psychic 'work' (e.g., by permitting an insult indirectly) and whether that economy plausibly produces pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish external vs internal hindrance
rubrics_metrics.description: Two cases: (1) gratification opposed by external hindrance (powerful persons, social position) which wit eludes, and (2) gratification opposed by an inner feeling/inhibition which wit removes; removal of internal hindrance often yields disproportionately higher pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging effect, note whether the joke's satisfaction overcomes social constraints (external) or moral/aesthetic/inhibitory restraints (internal). Internal-inhibition relief typically produces stronger comedic reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (rediscovery of the familiar) as pleasure-source
rubrics_metrics.description: One source of pleasure is discovering something familiar where one expected something new; 'recognition' or 'rediscovery' is pleasurable and often exploited by wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the joke produces a pleasurable 'aha' by revealing a familiar relation, and whether it intensifies this by briefly damming recognition and then releasing it (as in puzzles/games).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor of actuality (timeliness) increases effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Witticisms that deal with actual persons, events or topical affairs (recent, absorbing interests) provide additional pleasure; their effect is often transient and fades as the topical interest dies down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider topicality: topical jokes may score high in immediacy but age; evaluate longevity versus momentary impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-sound focus (sound over sense) and word-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Directing the psychic focus upon the sound instead of the sense (puns, homophones, similar-sounding words) economizes psychic effort and produces pleasure; examples include 'Home-Roulard' and translator/traitor examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate 'poor' jokes that rely only on sound (no senseful association) from 'good' jokes where sound similarity also produces or coincides with a meaningful semantic similarity. Good puns both shortcut thought and produce a concurrent sensible connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification / repetition / manifold application / modification of idioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques that reveal the familiar (repetition, alliteration, refrain, modification of idioms, manifold application) afford pleasure by making one find the familiar where one expected the new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how repetition or modified idioms create recognition and whether they serve an economy of psychic expenditure rather than mere mechanical trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity and false logic as facilitation of psychic economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques such as absurdity, false logic, displacement, and representation through the opposite make it easier to change thought-tracks and conserve psychic expenditure; absurdity can restore 'old liberties' and relieve intellectual pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether seemingly illogical or absurd connections actually produce economy/relief and therefore pleasure, rather than being merely nonsensical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement as a technical device
rubrics_metrics.description: Displacement (substituting one target or domain for another) is used to express otherwise unacceptable wishes or demands indirectly (e.g., shnorrer story—'nothing is too expensive for my health').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the displacement cleverly redirects tension to a permissible target, thereby producing satisfaction without overt transgression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation through the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique where the opposite is presented (e.g., calling a truth a lie), often used in skeptical witticisms to attack the certainty of knowledge or accepted notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the inversion exposes conceptual uncertainty or hypocrisy and whether this contributes to the joke's intellectual bite and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion and omission as powerful technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusions (to people/events) and omission (leaving out material that the hearer supplies) serve as strong technical devices; e.g., 'A wife is like an umbrella...' uses omission and allusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the hearer's shared knowledge base: allusion-rich jokes gain potency when the audience supplies the omitted link; failure to share that knowledge weakens the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good vs poor joke criterion (simultaneous meaningful association)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'poor' joke reaches the other idea only by sound similarity with no simultaneous senseful association; a 'good' joke produces both a short route and a meaningful, essential similarity in content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating word-jokes, require that the resulting association be sensible (not only phonetic). The best jokes combine the quick mental shortcut with a meaningful correspondence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual rhetorical/performative delivery matters (raconteur skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon, timing, and the raconteur's skill (ability to represent details through a trifle, to use tone and pacing) are necessary to produce laughter even when technical means are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include delivery and rhetorical skill when assessing a joke's effectiveness; some examples are 'technically nothing more than an illustration' but require the teller's art to elicit laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical witticism attacks certainty of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeptical witticisms do not target persons or institutions but the certainty of our knowledge; they exploit paradoxes about truth and interpretation (e.g., the liar/truth paradox in travel example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appraise whether the joke successfully foregrounds epistemic uncertainty and whether that abstraction yields amusement for the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in nonsense and the reproduction of old liberties
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an enduring pleasure in 'nonsense' (word experiment, reduplication) especially visible in children, intoxicated adults, or certain pathological states; wit can re-create these freedoms to yield pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contexts where nonsense is permissible or therapeutic (student revels, intoxication). Nonsense may be a deliberate device to relieve inhibitions rather than mere incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age/longevity of witticisms depends on topical tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Many witticisms have a flourishing season dependent on topical interest; once the underlying affair loses tension, the wit loses part of its pleasurable effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ephemeral topical witticisms from structurally enduring ones; longevity favors jokes whose pleasure-source is technique/recognition rather than mere actuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of remoteness between linked ideas increases pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure resulting from linking two idea-series by word or association appears greater the more remote and foreign the two series are to each other (greater economy achieved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, note how distant the linked semantic domains are; bigger cognitive 'short-circuit' often yields greater amusement if the connection is felicitous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Border-line wit: when truth is too explicit it weakens wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that merely express an ugly or cynical truth without sufficient technical disguise become 'border-line' and may lose laughter because the understanding is too exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective tendency-wit often requires a 'facade'—omission, allusion or technical artifice—to mask directness; evaluate whether the joke provides such a facade or bluntly states the truth.
